column2: A lion's crown or a horse's hairstyle that has never once seen a pair of scissors.
A metal grate over heat, or the fastest way to give a steak those appetising stripes.
Theatrical makeup that lets an actor become someone else entirely, at least until the curtain falls.
A miserable viral infection that comes with a fever and aches, and politely cancels all your weekend plans.
A hot drink of rum, water and spices — the Royal Navy's classic winter warmer.
Nature's own light-and-sound show, complete with lightning, thunder and a soaking.
The dramatic acoustic boom that follows a flash of lightning.
An old English silver coin, now remembered mostly when something isn't worth one.
The upper front part of the torso, doing the vital job of keeping your ribs, heart and lungs safe.
Heavy goods carried by ship, plane or lorry — anything that makes transport earn its keep.
The top layer of earth where plants take root and builders lay foundations.
A sweet, juicy fruit whose unmistakable bottom-heavy silhouette needs no introduction.
When an internal organ pushes through a weak spot in the muscle — definitely a job for a doctor, not Google.
A long, narrow raised strip of land, or a neat row of earth in the vegetable patch.
What you get when earth meets rain, and the main reason welcome mats exist.
An opaque, matte watercolour paint that forgives most artistic mistakes, except a dirty brush.
A hearty Hungarian meat stew rich with paprika — ideally nothing like the school canteen version.
A dashing light cavalryman of old, famous for braided jackets and magnificent moustaches.
The gritty sediment at the bottom of a cup that leaves tea-leaf readers thoroughly unimpressed.
A venomous Eurasian snake best admired from a very safe distance.
The stretch of space between two points, or everything the horizon keeps out of reach.
A polite title for a woman, or the queen in a deck of cards.
A massive barrier built across a river to hold back water and keep everyone's cellars dry.
A forced payment to a conqueror — history's version of an involuntary subscription.
A present given freely, or a natural talent that still expects years of practice.
A specific day on the calendar — handy for not turning up to a party a week early.
A hinged barrier in a wall, and the sole reason knocking was invented.
The left-hand side of an accounting ledger, recording money coming in or assets going up.
An outdated medical term that is now just a rather blunt insult.
A short, punchy phrase summing up a life philosophy, fit for a family crest or a Monday morning.
A large seagoing vessel built for journeys where the horizon is just a starting point.
Your parent's father — the undisputed owner of the best armchair and the tallest tales.
The resonant wooden plate of a stringed instrument that turns faint vibrations into actual music.
The head of a university faculty, whose office is where timetables and complaints collide.
The furnishings and finishing touches that turn an empty room into somewhere you actually want to sit.
Trade, work, or one's personal affairs — frequently none of yours, as the saying goes.
Government by the people, usually involving a ballot box and a polite British queue.
Twenty-four hours, or the bright bit between dawn and dusk spent discussing the weather.
Coins, notes or numbers on a screen that always seem to leave faster than they arrive.
An elected representative sent to parliament to speak on the voters' behalf — often at great length.
A small rural community where traffic jams are replaced by cockerels and lively local gossip.
An ornamental shrub prized for its bright red or yellow winter stems — the garden's cold-weather fireworks.
A slab of grass and matted roots ready to roll out as a lawn, or dried peat burned on an Irish hearth.
The pink tissue holding your teeth in place that your dentist insists on poking every six months.
A tiny horizontal mark that joins words together quietly, without making a scene like the dash.
A musical style built on syncopation and improvisation, where wrong notes are just bold choices.
Fruit boiled with sugar into a thick spread — the undisputed star of any British village fete.
A lively Scottish or Irish folk dance where the feet clearly move faster than the brain.
A juniper-flavoured spirit that, paired with tonic, is Britain's traditional answer to a long day.
A magical spirit from Arabian folklore who grants wishes with dangerously tricky small print.
A rugged four-wheel-drive vehicle built to keep going long after the tarmac gives up.
A musical symbol raising a note by a semitone — looks just like a tiny hashtag.
A strict eating plan under which the fridge becomes hostile territory, especially on Friday nights.
An electronic component that acts like a one-way street for electric current.
A flat, circular object found in record collections, sporting events and the human spine.
The screen of an electronic device where your computer silently judges your open tabs.
A young human being, and the person genuinely in charge of the household.
Wild birds or animals hunted for sport and the table — a staple of country-house dinners and murder mysteries.
The measurement from end to end, which on a motorway diversion is always longer than advertised.
The bottom surface of a car or ship, rarely seen until a mechanic looks at it and sighs.
The lowest point of a container, the sea, or one's patience.
A logical reason used to back up an opinion, or a noisy disagreement over dinner.
A rigid belief laid down as absolute truth, with zero tolerance for follow-up questions.
Water falling from the clouds — the backbone of British weather and the reason umbrellas go missing.
A carefully measured amount of medicine where freelancing is strongly discouraged.
A stint of guard duty, or the shift worked by those who don't get to go to bed on time.
A port worker who loads and unloads ships — the only person heavy cargo crates actually obey.
A medical practitioner or a top academic; either way, you'll probably be kept waiting.
A lengthwise groove forged into a sword blade to lighten it without sacrificing strength.
Money or a favour you owe — the one thing that never forgets your address.
A building to live in, and the destination that always beats the journey home.
A website's human-friendly address, sparing us all from memorising strings of IP numbers.
A towering industrial furnace that smelts iron ore around the clock at ferocious heat.
Someone who gives blood or an organ — a quiet hero rewarded with a cup of tea and a biscuit.
A formal accusation made to the authorities, capable of ruining friendships faster than gossip.
A paved route connecting places while thoroughly testing your car's suspension.
A flat plank of wood, or the dark classroom surface once covered in chalk dust.
Free time away from work, ideally spent relaxing rather than standing in a queue.
A small, thick-walled concrete bunker from wartime, now mostly a landmark for dog walkers.
Money earned from work or investments — reliably slower on the way in than on the way out.
A female child in relation to her parents, who will eventually inherit the TV remote.
A messy, noisy fistfight where words have clearly failed.
Slow, aimless movement carried by wind or current — also a popular winter driving style.
A tool for boring holes, traditionally operated by your neighbour at eight on a Sunday morning.
A light, pleasant half-sleep best achieved in an armchair with the television murmuring.
An involuntary tremble from cold, fear or excitement — in Britain, almost certainly the cold.
A speckled woodland songbird famous for repeating its musical phrases.
A yellow-flowered shrub that gave the Plantagenet royal dynasty its name.
A hefty, long-legged steppe bird, happily making a comeback on Salisbury Plain.
Someone bound to you by trust and affection, permitted to ring you at truly inconvenient hours.
A cluster of crystals lining a rock cavity — nature showing off without a designer.
A priest and scholar of the ancient Celts, now seen mostly in white robes at Stonehenge.
An exact twin, a cinema stunt stand-in, or a pub order that means business.
A smooth curve forming part of a circle, seen in geometry textbooks and rainbows.
A simple wind instrument with finger holes — notoriously effective at clearing towns of rats.
A hinged side piece on a pair of spectacles that hooks over your ear, or the limb attached to your shoulder.
An old European gold coin from the days when a purse actually jingled with real wealth.
The business end of a gun barrel — never a sensible thing to stare down.
A cosy cavity inside an old tree trunk, serving as prime real estate for owls and squirrels.
The spiritual essence of a person, or the emotional depth you put into good music.
A formal combat between two rivals at dawn to settle a matter of wounded honour.
A musical piece for two performers — a conversation that works only if neither interrupts.
A cloud of ash and gas rising from a fire, or Britain's classic excuse to step outside a pub.
A large, sweet summer fruit that smells wonderful long before you find a sharp knife.
An empty gap right in the middle of something that was supposed to be solid.
A narrowed spout at the end of a hose or pipe that directs a jet of liquid or gas.
An imperial unit equal to 2.54 centimetres — Britain's last stubborn stand against the metric system.
A shifting hill of sand sculpted by the wind, moving house without a single lorry.
Your parent's brother, reliably ready with a story involving either fishing or the war.
A bird with a chisel-like beak that hammers tree trunks for insects — nature's percussionist.
The warden of a sporting estate who knows every inch of the woods better than the map does.
Anything nutritious we eat to stay alive, and the main topic of conversation while eating it.
The act of travelling on horseback or a bicycle, requiring balance and a healthy dose of caution.
Someone sitting in the saddle or on a bike — an active pilot rather than mere luggage.
A neat evergreen conifer with drooping cones that gets dressed up in tinsel once a year.
